Title: Advanced machine learning techniques for predicting power generation and fault detection in solar photovoltaic systems

Abstract
This study investigated the application of advanced Machine Learning techniques to predict power generation and
detect abnormalities in solar Photovoltaic systems. The study conducted a comprehensive assessment of various
sophisticated models, including Random Trees, Random Forest, eXtreme Gradient Boosting, Linear Regression,
Gradient Boosting (GB), and Categorical Boosting (CatBoost), utilizing a substantial dataset of 97,333 sets. The
analysis focused on two fundamental objectives: power prediction and fault identiﬁcation, both of which are
crucial for enhancing the effectiveness and dependability of PV systems. CatBoost and GB models exhibited
exceptional performance in power prediction, with the maximum R-squared value of 0.994. Demonstrating a
strong correlation with the data and the ability to account for a substantial amount of the variation in power
generation. These models outperformed others by providing more accurate and reliable projections, which are
crucial for effective solar energy management and planning. CatBoost demonstrated superior performance
compared to other approaches in the ﬂaw detection test, attaining the highest performance metrics. The model
achieved an accuracy of 0.999743, precision of 0.997171, recall of 0.999291, and an F1 score of 0.998230. The
measures illustrated CatBoost’s exceptional ability to precisely identify problems with little errors, conﬁrming it
as the most successful model among those evaluated. The exceptional precision and dependability of the Cat-
Boost model in identifying faults highlighted its capacity for continuously monitoring and maintaining solar
systems in real-time, consequently augmenting operational efﬁciency. The study emphasized the signiﬁcance of
choosing suitable models to achieve the highest level of accuracy in predicting and detecting faults, thereby
enabling the development of more sustainable and efﬁcient solar energy systems. Subsequent research should
prioritize the validation of these models using varied datasets, integration of up-to-date meteorological data, and
creation of defect detection methods in real-time to enhance system efﬁciency.

1 Introduction
The energy crisis worldwide and climate change demand the use of Renewable Energy Sources (RES). RES,
particularly solar energy, are a good choice due to their abundant availability and long-term power production
capabilities. Solar energy is recognized [1, 2] as a sustainable and inexhaustible resource and is an important part
of future energy strategy. Technological improvements, cost reductions, and favorable government policies help
propel the global proliferation of Photovoltaic (PV) systems. All over the world, nations are investing heavily in
PV technology for increasing energy security, decreasing greenhouse gas emissions, as well as transitioning to
more sustainable energy systems [3, 4]. This results in the crucial need for efﬁcient methods of power generation
and reliable fault detection techniques to ensure system performance and reliability as the number of PV
installations signiﬁcantly increases [5, 6].

Robust fault detection and diagnosis procedures are necessary to ensure the efﬁciency and reliability of PV
systems. Defects in PV systems can result in substantial reductions in energy output and higher expenses for
maintenance, jeopardizing the overall sustainability of solar power generation. Timely diagnosis and repair of
issues is crucial for boosting the operating efﬁciency and reliability of PV installations. Advanced monitoring and
fault detection systems can achieve this [7, 8]. By incorporating advanced Machine Learning (ML) methods into
fault detection systems, their accuracy and effectiveness are enhanced, resulting in minimal disturbance and
optimal performance of PV systems [9, 10].
Overseeing PV systems presents numerous difﬁculties, mostly stemming from the ﬂuctuating power pro-
duction resulting from shifting weather patterns and technological malfunctions. The variability of solar energy,
which includes factors like cloud cover, temperature variations, and shading, signiﬁcantly impacts the stability
and dependability of PV systems [11, 12]. Furthermore, technical concerns such as connection problems, inverter
malfunctions, and panel degradation further complicate the administration of PV systems [13].
These problems signiﬁcantly impact the total efﬁciency and maintenance expenses of PV systems. The need
for advanced monitoring and control systems arises due to frequent variations in power production in order to
ensure optimal performance. This not only ampliﬁes the intricacy of operations but also escalates the expenses
linked to maintenance and rectiﬁcation of faults [14]. However, inadequate diagnosis or control of defects can
severely waste energy, rendering the use of solar power installations economically unfeasible. Researchers today
are addressing these issues by using ML and Deep Learning (DL) to identify and predict ﬂaws. These solutions
improve the accuracy of power generation forecasting and anomaly detection, resulting in higher reliability and
efﬁciency in PV systems [15, 16].
The integration of ML algorithms into the forecasting of power generation and identiﬁcation of anomalies in
PV systems represents a signiﬁcant leap in the handling of renewable energy resources. ML models analyze the
PV system performance data using advanced algorithms and large amounts of data to uncover intricate patterns.
They can predict energy output very accurately and can detect potential issues with a high level of precision
[9, 17]. The beneﬁts of ML for PV systems cover areas of forecasting with greater precision and detection of
faults. The continuous monitoring of PV systems offered by these methods is fundamental to maximizing
performance and minimizing the downtime caused by problems. A real-time monitoring system is able to notify
operators about abnormalities in a blink of an eye so that they can take quick corrective measures [18]. Further,
the adoption of ML brings predictive maintenance into play that most certainly cuts down operation expenditure.
Through very accurate forecasting of the timing and location of defects, these systems are able to proactively plan
for maintenance actions, avoiding surprise malfunctions and extending the useful life of PV components [19, 20].
The main purpose of this study is to evaluate the functionality of various advanced ML models in predicting
power generation and diagnosing defects in PV systems. This research aims to ﬁnd the most suitable models that
will improve the performance and dependability of PV systems, contributing to more effective and sustainable
solar energy solutions. This study involves the analysis of a substantial dataset, comprising 97,333 sets of
observations from a PV system. What this dataset provides is voltages, currents, power output, inverter tem-
perature, daily energy generation, and system uptime. This study uses the following ML models for power
prediction and fault detection, as summarized in Table 1. Results of this research will improve the understanding
of the application of ML to enhance the efﬁciency and reliability of solar energy systems, leading to advancement
in renewable energy technology.

2 Literature review
2.1 Previous studies
The literature review provides a comprehensive summary of prior research on the application of ML techniques in
PV systems, focusing on both power prediction and fault detection. As Table 2 details, this is organized in a way
that allows each study to be clear and compared to the others. The discussion of the research presents the
algorithms employed in the research, the performance metrics used for evaluation, and the main ﬁndings of each
study. Moreover, it presents the domains that have been explored in these studies and the associated limitations
faced in these studies, to provide a context of the scope and boundaries of previous efforts in this domain.
Through synthesizing this information, Table 2 provides a consolidated reference to assess the progress and
challenges in the ﬁeld, and serves as a foundation to push the ﬁeld further.
A short-term PV power forecasting model was developed by Radhi et al. [21] using Artiﬁcial Neural Networks
(ANNs) optimized by Genetic Algorithm (GA) and Gray Wolf Optimization (GWO) techniques. Real-time data
collected on a PV prototype in Iraq under varying atmospheric conditions (sunny, cloudy, rainy) was used in the
study. Metrics such as R2, Mean Absolute Errors (MAE), Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), and Mean Squared
Error (MSE) were used to evaluate performance, and the ANN-GA model outperformed with R2 values greater
than 0.89 in all conditions. In this model, the variations in solar irradiance were well captured and the model
provided better prediction accuracy than traditional ANN and ANN-GWO methods. A limitation of the study is
that it is limited to region speciﬁc data and input variables, and does not include things like humidity and dust,
which would increase prediction accuracy.
Lavador-Osorio et al. [22] looked into how to use Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) and k-Nearest Neighbor
(k-NN) together to ﬁnd and pinpoint Open Circuit Faults (OCF) in PV systems. Using nighttime measurements
and pulsed red light at 10 kHz, the approach achieved high predictability (90–93%) across different PV array
conﬁgurations (4 9 1, 4 9 2, 5 9 1, and 5 9 2). The method is scalable for larger systems, as fault localization
accuracy improves with size. While effective, its reliance on nighttime conditions and speciﬁc pulsation settings
may limit broader application.
In the study of Yang and Faizan [23], a Long Short-Term Memory Feedforward Neural Network (LSTM-
FFNN) model was proposed that is coupled with Decision Trees (DT), Support Vector Machine (SVM), and
Linear Regression (LR) for PV fault detection. Using voltage current data under varying irradiance, the method
effectively classiﬁed eight fault types with high accuracy and robustness in complex conditions. It, however,
requires substantial computational resources and detailed voltage current data.

In photovoltaic power plants (PVPPs), Kollarov and Ostrenko [24] used classical ML methods, such as SVM
and Random Forest (RF), to forecast energy generation. The study addressed the problem of weather induced data
irregularities and optimized feature choices to reduce error. High performance was demonstrated by results, with
Area Under the Curve (AUC) approaching 1, enabling effective energy system integration and resource man-
agement. Nevertheless, the ML models were tuned carefully enough to cope with complex patterns and to make
reliable predictions.
Binary Adaptive eXtreme Gradient Boosting (BA-XGBoost) was implemented by Suliman et al. [25] for the
task of detecting electrical faults in PV arrays and achieved the highest accuracy (87.56%) among all methods.
BA-XGBoost performed well in accuracy and fault detection reliability, but at cost of higher computational time
compared to other classiﬁers.
Aldosari et al. [26] compared ML models for power prediction at a 300 MW solar farm in Saudi Arabia. The
SVM with RBF performed the best among such SVMs with Radial Basis Function (RBF), polynomial, linear, and
sigmoid kernels, DT, and DL models with 98% accuracy, 97% precision and AUC of 0.99 in all power classes.
DL and DT models worked well, but the SVM with a sigmoid kernel was the worst. The work demonstrates that
SVM with RBF is effective at ﬁnding nonlinear patterns, but only on data from one solar farm.

ML and Ensemble Learning (EL) based PV system forecasting and fault diagnosis were developed by Kar-
thikeyan and Jagadeeshwaran (2023) [27] in the Machine Learning-based PV Prediction and Fault Analysis
System (ML-PVPFAS). The proposed ML-PVPFAS achieved MAPE of 4.93, RMSE of 4.64, accuracy of
90.31%, precision of 93.60%, and computation time of 77.64 ms, showing its efﬁciency in PV power output
prediction and complex fault identiﬁcation.
In the case of six PV technologies, power outputs were predicted by ensemble based ML models such as
Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM) and RF, as evaluated by Raj et al. (2023) [28]. They used data from a
1.2 MW solar farm over three years and found GBM and RF had superior performance with low RMSE of
17.59 kW and 17.14 kW, as well as MAE of 8.28 kW and 7.88 kW respectively. Results were constrained by PV
technology types and regional settings; however, these models were computationally efﬁcient, allowing for real
time predictions.
In Zou et al. (2020) [29], a day ahead PV power prediction hybrid model based on Similar Day Analysis
(SDA), GA and Extreme Learning Machine (ELM) was proposed. The SDA-GA-ELM model employs Pearson
correlation to ﬁnd similar training days, and incorporates historical power data, meteorological factors. ELMs are
optimized by GA to increase accuracy and efﬁciency. On real world data from the Desert Knowledge Australia
Solar Center, the model produced high R2, low MAE and Normalized Root Mean Square Error (NRMSE).
However, it has limited generalization, as it relies on SDA.

3.2 Machine learning algorithms
Table 4 presents a succinct juxtaposition of the ML algorithms chosen for our research article, emphasizing their
classiﬁcations, advantages, and disadvantages. The algorithms provided are Random Trees (RT), RF, eXtreme
Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Linear Regression, Gradient Boosting (GB), and Categorical Boosting (CatBoost).
Each algorithm possesses distinct advantages. For example, RT is straightforward to read and efﬁcient, whereas
RF exhibits superior accuracy and resilience against overﬁtting. XGBoost is renowned for its exceptional per-
formance and ability to effectively handle missing values, whereas Linear Regression is highly regarded for its
straightforwardness and ability to be easily interpreted. GB is especially efﬁcient when dealing with structured
data and offers a high degree of accuracy. However, CatBoost is renowned for its capacity to effectively manage
categorical data and its resilience. Due to their multitude of qualities, they are highly suitable candidates for our
research on power generation and fault detection in solar systems. This is because they collectively provide a
broad range of instruments to tackle various aspects of the problem. Therefore, the study used these method-
ologies to ensure a thorough and effective analysis in our research.
This study employed a full workﬂow, which is illustrated in Fig. 8, for data processing, model training, and
evaluation. The study imports the necessary libraries and loads the dataset. Afterwards, the dataset undergoes data
exploration and visualization tools to get a more profound comprehension of its contents. The next phase involves
data preparation for ML models. Subsequently, the process bifurcates into two distinct branches: one devoted to
power prediction and the other concentrated on fault identiﬁcation. Each discipline encompasses methodologies
for formulating evaluation functions, evaluating regression models, and scrutinizing classiﬁcation models. The
regression models are trained and evaluated, with the results recorded in a Comma-Separated Values (CSV) ﬁle
and the model’s performance illustrated graphically. The process for classifying models involves training and
assessing the models, storing the classiﬁcation results in a CSV ﬁle, and graphically displaying the model’s
performance. The workﬂow terminates at the ﬁnal step. The use of this method guarantees a methodical and
comprehensive examination, enabling accurate power estimation and identiﬁcation of faults in PV systems.

to strike a balance between these two measurements. This relationship is mathematically represented by Eq. (7).

4 Results and discussion
4.1 Power generation model performance results
Table 5 presents the performance indicators of various models used in predicting power generation. These metrics
are calculated from a dataset consisting of 97,333 pieces of data. Table 5 displays a progressive arrangement of
the models according to their increasing efﬁciency. The given information includes the MSE, RMSE, and R2
values for each model.
The RT model demonstrates a maximum MSE of 84,000, a maximum RMSE of 289.358, and a minimum R2
value of 0.987. These ﬁndings suggest that the RT model is the least effective in calculating power in this speciﬁc
situation. The RF and XGBoost models have similar performance, resulting in MSE values of around 42,000. The
RF and XGBoost models have RMSE values of roughly 205.906 and 205.852, respectively. Both models achieve
an R2 value of 0.993.
The models of Linear Regression, GB, and CatBoost exhibit exceptional performance. The Linear Regression
model has a MSE of 41,000, a RMSE of 202.591, and a R2 of 0.994. GB demonstrates superior performance, with
an MSE of 40,000, an RMSE of 200.170, and an R2 of 0.994. The CatBoost model has superior performance
compared to other models, achieving the lowest MSE of 40,000, the lowest RMSE of 198.822, and the greatest
R2 value of 0.994.
The results demonstrate the efﬁcacy of GB and CatBoost models in properly forecasting power generation,
with CatBoost exhibiting the highest overall performance among the assessed models. The high R2 values seen in
the majority of the models indicate a robust ﬁt to the data, while the lower MSE and RMSE values reﬂect accurate
predictions. This analysis emphasizes the need of selecting appropriate models to attain the utmost accuracy in
forecasting power generation operations.
Based on the data shown in Table 5, the RMSE values for the models exhibit a range of roughly 200. Given
that the dataset includes power values that can reach up to 10,000, an RMSE of approximately 200 indicates a
rather small margin of error. To be more exact, this shows that the forecasts have an average deviation of 2% from
the greatest power, which demonstrates a good level of accuracy. Given that the dataset comprises 97,333 sets,
the elevated R2 values, all of which are near 1, provide additional evidence that the models effectively account for
a signiﬁcant amount of the variability in the data. Hence, the RMSE values presented in Table 5 indicate that the
models are effectively predicting power generation, with errors that are negligible compared to the size of the
dataset.

5 Limitation and future work
PV technology is crucial in the global transition to sustainable energy, offering a renewable, cost-effective, and
environmentally friendly solution to reducing greenhouse gas emissions and combating climate change.
The investigation has produced encouraging outcomes in both power forecasting and fault identiﬁcation.
Nevertheless, there exist certain constraints that need to be resolved in future research in order to further improve
the durability and practicality of the suggested approaches. A drawback is the dependence on a solitary dataset
consisting of 97,333 items. Although this dataset contains a signiﬁcant quantity of data for training and evaluating
models, the performance of these models may vary when applied to datasets from various solar systems or
geographical regions with distinct climatic circumstances. Subsequent research should involve conducting tests
on varied datasets to evaluate the models’ capacity to apply to different situations. Another constraint is the

6 Conclusion
The results of this study represent the use of sophisticated ML methods in forecasting power generation and
identifying malfunctions in solar PV systems with great accuracy. On a dataset containing 97,333 sets, this study
assessed multiple models, including RT, RF, XGBoost, Linear Regression, GB, and CatBoost. The results
showed that the CatBoost and GB models had outstanding performance on both fault detection and power
prediction tasks. Power prediction models as well as fault detection models, according to these models, achieved
impressive accuracy, precision, recall and F1 scores, and modest MSE and RMSE values respectively. These
ﬁndings highlight the possibility of using ML to improve the effectiveness and dependability of solar systems,
thereby contributing to the development of more environmentally friendly energy options. The high R2 values
seen in the majority of the models indicate a robust alignment with the data, thereby proving the models’ capacity
to elucidate a signiﬁcant proportion of the variability in power generation. This study emphasizes the signiﬁcance
of choosing suitable models to achieve the highest level of accuracy in prediction and the ability to detect faults
effectively. Although the results are encouraging, it is essential to evaluate these models using a wide range of
datasets and in different climatic situations to assure their strength and applicability. Furthermore, by integrating
up-to-the-minute weather data, creating defect detection methods that operate in real-time, and investigating
transfer learning approaches, the performance of the model could be further improved. Future directions of equal
importance include improving model interpretability and exploring scalability to larger datasets. In summary, this
research offers a thorough assessment of sophisticated ML models, showcasing their ability to greatly enhance
power generation forecasts and identify faults in solar PV systems, serving as a stepping stone for integrating
more sophisticated techniques in future studies. The knowledge acquired from this study establishes the foun-
dation for future progress and breakthroughs in the sector, ultimately leading to the development of renewable
energy technology.

Abstract: This study investigated the application of advanced Machine Learning techniques to predict power generation and detect abnormalities in solar Photovoltaic systems. The study conducted a comprehensive assessment of various sophisticated models, including Random Trees, Random Forest, eXtreme Gradient Boosting, Linear Regression, Gradient Boosting (GB), and Categorical Boosting (CatBoost), utilizing a substantial dataset of 97,333 sets. The analysis focused on two fundamental objectives: power prediction and fault identiﬁcation, both of which are crucial for enhancing the effectiveness and dependability of PV systems. CatBoost and GB models exhibited exceptional performance in power prediction, with the maximum R-squared value of 0.994. Demonstrating a strong correlation with the data and the ability to account for a substantial amount of the variation in power generation. These models outperformed others by providing more accurate and reliable projections, which are crucial for effective solar energy management and planning. CatBoost demonstrated superior performance compared to other approaches in the ﬂaw detection test, attaining the highest performance metrics. The model achieved an accuracy of 0.999743, precision of 0.997171, recall of 0.999291, and an F1 score of 0.998230. The measures illustrated CatBoost’s exceptional ability to precisely identify problems with little errors, conﬁrming it as the most successful model among those evaluated. The exceptional precision and dependability of the Cat- Boost model in identifying faults highlighted its capacity for continuously monitoring and maintaining solar systems in real-time, consequently augmenting operational efﬁciency. The study emphasized the signiﬁcance of choosing suitable models to achieve the highest level of accuracy in predicting and detecting faults, thereby enabling the development of more sustainable and efﬁcient solar energy systems. Subsequent research should prioritize the validation of these models using varied datasets, integration of up-to-date meteorological data, and creation of defect detection methods in real-time to enhance system efﬁciency.
